text: CONTEXT

text: Why Grad Students, of All People?
html: Why Grad Students, of All People?

text: This started as a class project on how AI is reshaping different fields — each of us was assigned a segment to dig into. Mine was postgraduate computer science students: master's and PhD candidates studying abroad.
html: This started as a class project on how AI is reshaping different fields — each of us was assigned a segment to dig into. Mine was postgraduate computer science students: master's and PhD candidates studying abroad.

text: It turned out to be a good draw. This group is close to a best-case scenario for AI adoption — technically fluent, research-heavy workloads, constant daily exposure to AI for both academic and applied work. If anyone had a clear, lived sense of where AI genuinely helps and where it quietly fails them, it would be this group.

text: METHOD
html: METHOD

text: Chasing Experience, Not Numbers
html: Chasing Experience, Not Numbers

text: What I needed wasn't a number. It was experience. Not just how often students use AI, but how it actually feels to use it: where it helps, where it quietly fails them, what they do when it lets them down. That kind of data doesn't live in a survey. It only comes out when someone talks, at length, in their own words. So the only real option was deep, one on one interviews.
html: What I needed wasn't a number. It was experience. Not just how often students use AI, but how it actually feels to use it: where it helps, where it quietly fails them, what they do when it lets them down. That kind of data doesn't live in a survey. It only comes out when someone talks, at length, in their own words. So the only real option was deep, one on one interviews.

text: I went through the transcripts twice. Once with an Affinity Diagram, letting patterns surface from the raw data on their own. That was the clearest sign it was time to stop and start synthesizing.

text: Six Things I Didn't Expect to Hear So Clearly
html: Six Things I Didn't Expect to Hear So Clearly

text: Six themes came out of the affinity mapping, clear enough that I didn't have to squint to see them. Here's what grad students actually told me, in their own words.
html: Six themes came out of the affinity mapping, clear enough that I didn't have to squint to see them. Here's what grad students actually told me, in their own words.

text: 1. Specific Tasks, Not General Chat
html: 1. Specific Tasks, Not General Chat

text: Every student I talked to used AI constantly, but not as a general chatbot. Their use cases were specific: paraphrasing dense text, debugging code, summarizing academic papers with dedicated tools. They'd already outgrown the "ask it anything" mindset. What they wanted was speed and precision inside a workflow, not a chatbot to explore with.
html: Every student I talked to used AI constantly, but not as a general chatbot. Their use cases were specific: paraphrasing dense text, debugging code, summarizing academic papers with dedicated tools. They'd already outgrown the "ask it anything" mindset. What they wanted was speed and precision inside a workflow, not a chatbot to explore with.

text: 🗯️❝ I often rely on AI to summarize articles or provide insights into complex topics, which saves me a lot of time.❞
html: 🗯️❝ I often rely on AI to summarize articles or provide insights into complex topics, which saves me a lot of time.❞

text: 2. The time saved is not small. It's dramatic
html: 2. The time saved is not small. It's dramatic

text: This wasn't a marginal efficiency gain. Students described AI turning multi day problems into a matter of hours.
html: This wasn't a marginal efficiency gain. Students described AI turning multi day problems into a matter of hours.

text: 🗯️❝ Instead of spending several days reading through documentation, I can resolve problems in just a few hours with AI.❞
html: 🗯️❝ Instead of spending several days reading through documentation, I can resolve problems in just a few hours with AI.❞

text: This is the strongest, clearest value in the whole study, and also the highest bar anything else has to clear. Anything that adds friction is competing against days becoming hours.
html: This is the strongest, clearest value in the whole study, and also the highest bar anything else has to clear. Anything that adds friction is competing against days becoming hours.

text: 3. Two very different walls: money and permission
html: 3. Two very different walls: money and permission

text: The barriers weren't really technical. They were structural. Cost was one. Premium tools are expensive enough that students described pooling resources just to get access.

text: 🗯️❝ It's quite expensive, but we're considering sharing an account to make it more manageable.❞

text: The other wall was institutional permission. Supervisors sometimes explicitly discouraged AI use, cutting students off from a tool they'd already come to depend on.
html: The other wall was institutional permission. Supervisors sometimes explicitly discouraged AI use, cutting students off from a tool they'd already come to depend on.

text: 🗯️❝ My manager doesn't allow us to use AI tools for our projects, which makes it difficult for me to get help.❞

text: THROUGH LINE
html: THROUGH LINE

text: What Do They Actually Want From AI?
html: What Do They Actually Want From AI?

text: Put these six things together and one pattern sits underneath all of them. Students don't want AI to think for them. They want it to take the friction out of the parts of the work that were never really the point: formatting, searching, first drafts. And they want it to stay out of the way of the parts where the thinking itself is the value.

text: The finding I trusted least turned out to be true for me too. I did the theme extraction the traditional way: days of full time work, sorting quotes by hand. It grouped the data into almost the exact same six patterns anyway, in minutes.

text: AN UPDATE, MONTHS LATER
html: AN UPDATE, MONTHS LATER

text: The Worry That Got an Answer!
html: The Worry That Got an Answer!

text: A few months after this research wrapped, one worry actually got an answer. OpenAI released Study Mode, a version of ChatGPT that asks guiding questions instead of handing over the answer. Not long after, Google released NotebookLM, built around the same idea: understanding the material, not just getting through it faster.
html: A few months after this research wrapped, one worry actually got an answer. OpenAI released Study Mode, a version of ChatGPT that asks guiding questions instead of handing over the answer. Not long after, Google released NotebookLM, built around the same idea: understanding the material, not just getting through it faster.

text: Neither was built because of this study, but they're aimed at exactly what participants were worried about: that leaning on AI for quick answers was quietly costing them their own understanding.
html: Neither was built because of this study, but they're aimed at exactly what participants were worried about: that leaning on AI for quick answers was quietly costing them their own understanding.

text: The other findings haven't aged the same way. The cost barrier is only partly lower, cheaper plans exist now, but so does account sharing, still. And the confident, sometimes wrong answers participants described back then? Still confident. Still sometimes wrong.
